name: Grace Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick orders at a big electronics fulfilment centre, phones, chargers, headphones, that kind of thing. Half the building is a robot zone where little orange robots carry whole shelves to the pickers, and the other half is old-style aisles, which is where I am. I walk about fifteen kilometres a shift with a trolley and a wrist scanner. Whenever they're short in the robot zone I put my hand up to cover it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The walking wears me out, and the fact that I'm still under the target rate because I miss shelf codes. What I like is the robot zone, honestly. I watch the maintenance guy, Marek, fixing them and I ask him a hundred questions. At night I ask an AI chatbot to explain the fault codes I saw, and my housemate Jess laughs at me for doing homework nobody set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what a waste of hype, and also, good, nobody loses their job over it. Online I'd probably post that the money should have gone into wages instead. At work I'd tell Marek his job is safe forever, and he'd roll his eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit gutted. I was counting on robots spreading so there'd be more maintenance jobs, and that's my way off the floor. If nothing changes, I stay a slow picker on low pay with a long walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going for the maintenance route anyway, because the robots in our zone aren't going anywhere. I'd sign up for the free online electrics basics course and keep shadowing Marek on my breaks. And I'd keep putting 20 a week into a jar, which is all I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless, and a bit trapped. Like the bus came and it wasn't mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound disappointed. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the change was my chance. I know that sounds odd from someone who's pro-union, but I'd rather the change happens and we fight over who gets the benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does money look like for you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. Rent with Jess, phone, bus pass, and I've maybe three weeks' worth saved. There are only two other big warehouses in town, and both pay worse than mine.

say: The AI hype was a **waste of money** that should have gone into **wages**.
At least nobody loses their job over it, which is good.
think: I'd be a bit **gutted**, because spreading robots were my route to **maintenance work**.
Without change, I stay a **slow picker** on low pay.
do: Sign up for the **free online electrics** basics course anyway.
Keep shadowing Marek on **breaks** to learn the robot repairs.
Put **20 a week** into a savings jar.
feel: **Restless** and a bit trapped, like the bus came and it wasn't mine.
S0.quote: I'd rather the change happens and we fight over who gets the benefits.
fieldNote: She's **disappointed** by the plateau, which is unusual and comes from her plan to move into robot maintenance.
Her **thin savings** and two worse-paying local warehouses keep her uneasy.
Pro-union but **pro-change**: she wants the fight to be over sharing gains.

steps.text: Take the free online electrics basics course and shadow Marek
Put 20 a week into a savings jar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get trained, and the company should pay for it. Online I'd share stuff about warehouses that retrained pickers as robot technicians. I'd also say unions need to bargain over training, not just pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly good if I move fast. The thinking stuff, like the rota planning, changes first, and the robots spread slowly, which means more machines that need people to fix them. If I'm still a picker when they reach my aisles, then it's bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the company's maintenance trainee scheme the first day it opens. I'd use AI tutoring every night to get through the electrics theory, because I left school early and the maths scares me. And I'd tell the union rep we want a training deal written into the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous excited. Like the first day at a new job, but I haven't got the job yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you asked anyone at work about moving to maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I asked Marek's manager in the summer. She said they only take people with a certificate, so that's why I'm doing the course. I'll go back with the paper in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the pickers who don't want to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry about them, properly. Big Pete in my aisle can't read the screens well, and he'd be the first one squeezed. That's why I'd push the union, because not everyone can jump like me.

say: This is the moment to **get trained**, and the company should pay for it.
Unions need to bargain over **training**, not just pay.
think: It's mostly **good for me** if I move fast into maintenance.
If I'm **still a picker** when robots reach my aisles, then it's bad.
do: Apply for the **maintenance trainee scheme** the day it opens.
Use **AI tutoring** every night for the electrics theory and maths.
Ask the union rep for a **training deal** in the contract.
feel: **Nervous and excited**, like a first day at a job I haven't got yet.
S1.quote: Big Pete in my aisle can't read the screens well, and he'd be the first one squeezed.
fieldNote: She sees slow robot spread as **more repair jobs**, and wants to be first in line.
Her daily **AI tutoring** is a practical crutch for the maths she missed at school.
Her progressive views show in concern for **slower colleagues**, not just herself.

steps.text: Apply for the company's robot maintenance trainee scheme on day one
Use an AI tutor nightly for electrics theory and maths
Ask the union rep to get a training deal into the contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for everyone, now, not in 2030. Training paid by the companies that profit, and income support for anyone who can't retrain. I'd be posting that and turning up to whatever union meeting there was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking stuff, five for the robots. For me, the thinking stuff barely matters, it's the robots that end the picking. So I have about five years to get off the floor, and with no savings that's tight but doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the technician certificate straight away, evenings and weekends, even if I have to pay for some of it. I'd use the AI to study and to practise fault-finding. I'd also look for any job in robot maintenance, even nights, anywhere within an hour on the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I'd rather be running than sitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about 2031. Are robot technicians safe after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. If AI can diagnose the faults and robots can fix robots, then maybe not for long. But somebody has to be there in the meantime, and I'd rather be that somebody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if you had to pay for a course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out, mostly. Jess and I have one night out a month, that'd go. I'd sell my old laptop too, and use the library computers.

say: We need a **plan for everyone** now, not in 2030.
Companies that profit should fund **training** and **income support** for those who can't retrain.
think: Robots end picking around **2031**, so I have about five years to get off the floor.
With **no savings**, that's tight but doable.
do: Start the **technician certificate** straight away, evenings and weekends.
Apply for any **robot maintenance** job within an hour by bus.
Drop nights out and **sell my old laptop** to fund the course.
feel: **Anxious but busy**, preferring to be running than sitting.
S2.quote: Two years for the thinking stuff, five for the robots. For me, the thinking stuff barely matters, it's the robots that end the picking.
fieldNote: She reads the **robot delay** clearly and plans around it rather than the AGI date.
She admits **technician jobs** may not last either, but still chooses action.
Her thin cushion means **cutting nights out** and selling a laptop to pay fees.

steps.text: Start the robot technician certificate on evenings and weekends
Apply for robot maintenance jobs within an hour by bus
Drop monthly nights out and sell her old laptop
Attend union meetings pushing for company-funded training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, with less shouting. I'd say we've got a window, so let's use it properly, with apprenticeships and paid training. I'd keep posting about warehouses that did it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AGI and eight for robots, so I'd have time to get qualified and get a few years of real experience. That makes me much more confident. The bigger worry is whether there are still enough technician jobs once the robots don't need much fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan, but I'd do it properly instead of in a panic. I'd finish the certificate in two years and get a trainee spot in maintenance. Then I'd learn the AI diagnostic tools as they come in, because the people who can run them will last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a small knot underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can save a little while I train, instead of selling everything. Maybe 30 a month. And I can do the course at a normal pace and not fail the maths because I rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move town for a technician job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if I had to. Jess will be finished with nursing by then and she could work anywhere. There's a big robot warehouse two hours north that's always hiring technicians.

say: We've got a **window**, so use it for **apprenticeships** and paid training.
I'd keep posting about warehouses that retrained their pickers well.
think: Eight years until robots gives me time to **qualify** and gain experience.
The bigger worry is whether enough **technician jobs** remain once robots need little fixing.
do: Finish the **certificate in two years** and win a maintenance trainee spot.
Learn the **AI diagnostic tools** as they arrive.
Save about **30 a month** while training.
S3.quote: There's a big robot warehouse two hours north that's always hiring technicians.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her plan from **panic** into a paced qualification route.
She still doubts the **long-term demand** for technicians, which keeps her anxious.
She'd **move** for work, with her housemate's nursing as flexible support.

steps.text: Finish the robot technician certificate within two years
Learn AI diagnostic tools as they arrive in maintenance
Save about 30 a month during training
Move two hours north for a technician job if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version, if governments use the time. I'd still push the union to plan now, because ten years disappears fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, I think. I'd have the certificate, years in maintenance and probably a better wage by the time robots really arrive. Thinking AI would change the planning side, but I'm not on that side anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, the electrics basics course and the trainee application, same as always. Then I'd save a bit more each year and maybe go further, into automation engineering at college. I'd use the AI tools every day like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is there a risk you'd relax too much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but not me. I get bored if I'm not learning something. My housemate Jess says I'm the only person she knows who reads robot manuals for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you like to be at 37?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leading a small maintenance team, living in a flat I don't share with three people, and still in a union. That would be a good life.

say: This is the **good version**, if governments use the time.
I'd still push the union to **plan now**, because ten years disappears fast.
think: I'd have the **certificate** and years in maintenance before robots really arrive.
Thinking AI changes planning work, but I'm **not on that side**.
do: Take the **electrics course** and the trainee application this year.
Save a bit more each year and consider **automation engineering** at college.
Keep using **AI tools** daily for study.
feel: **Calm**, mostly, and even a bit excited.
S4.quote: My housemate Jess says I'm the only person she knows who reads robot manuals for fun.
fieldNote: With a decade, the change looks **good for her**, so she's genuinely calm.
Her hopes are **specific**: lead a maintenance team, her own flat.
She stays **pro-union** even as she plans to rise.

steps.text: Take the electrics course and later study automation engineering
Apply for the maintenance trainee scheme this year
Save a little more each year from her pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to rush the course with no money behind me. What would help is a paid apprenticeship, where you earn while you learn, and the company has to take pickers, not just people who already have papers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask if we want the change. Everyone assumes pickers hate robots. I don't, I just want to be the one fixing them, not the one shown the door.

headlineQuote: Everyone assumes pickers hate robots. I don't, I just want to be the one fixing them, not the one shown the door.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old picker** at an electronics warehouse with a robot zone, still under the target rate.
She has **three weeks** of savings, shares a flat with Jess, and few local warehouses pay as well.
She uses **AI daily** to study and wants to become a robot maintenance technician.
She's **pro-union and pro-change**, wanting workers to share the gains and slower colleagues protected.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have to rush training with no money behind her.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** where companies must take pickers without existing qualifications.
